Architecture (no links, just the concepts):

Most humanoids run centralized compute—single Jetson Orin or x86 board in the torso.
Motor controllers are distributed (each joint has a microcontroller handling low-level servo loops), but they're dumb—just following commands from central brain.
CAN bus or EtherCAT ties it all together.

The embodied brain split you're intuiting is real.

Research calls it S1/S2 or "body brain" vs "planning brain":
S1 (body brain): Runs at 50-100Hz.
Handles balance, reflexes, motor primitives, force feedback.
Trained via imitation learning or RL on physical tasks.
This is where behavior cloning lives—the stuff that knows *how* to crack an egg given force parameters.
- S2 (planning brain): Runs at 1-5Hz.
LLM or VLA that interprets intent, breaks down tasks, provides parameters to S1.
"Crack the egg gently into the bowl" → translates to force envelope, approach vector, grip pressure → hands off to S1.
Everything Stack fits here directly.

- Versionable: Behavior policies version like any other component.
Roll back if a new training run makes the arm worse at something.
- Cross-platform persistence: ObjectBox stores the learned trajectories, sensor logs, success/failure outcomes.
The dual-persistence pattern you just finished means you could prototype in web (simulation) and deploy to native (real robot).

Build vs buy right now:

Power: Electric motors, battery in torso.

Electric actuators with high-ratio gearboxes or direct drive are the standard now.
Why you'd want hydraulics: Raw power.
Lifting heavy things, explosive movements like jumping.
For home tasks?
Electric handles everything you'd actually want.
3D printing hydraulics: Technically possible but not practical.
You can print channels and housings, but seals are the problem.
FDM layer lines leak under pressure.
Resin prints are brittle.
You'd need machined aluminum cylinders with proper O-ring grooves.
Max pressure on printed parts is maybe 100-200 PSI before failure.
Real hydraulics run 3000+ PSI.
What you CAN 3D print: Structural brackets, sensor mounts, gripper fingers, link housings.
The SO-100/SO-101 kits are mostly 3D printed frames with off-the-shelf servos.
That's the sweet spot—print the structure, buy the actuation.

Handles temporal coherence.

Here's the actual stack:

Classical (matrix math, no learning):
Inverse kinematics: "Put end effector here" → solve for joint angles.
Pure linear algebra.
- PID controllers: Low-level servo loops.
No neural net.
- Dynamics models: Physics equations predicting how robot moves given torques.

Neural (learned):
Vision processing: What am I looking at?
- Task planning: What sequence of actions accomplishes this goal?
- Behavior policies: Given current state, what's the next action?
The trend is end-to-end neural.
VLAs (Vision-Language-Action models) skip the classical middle layers entirely.
Camera pixels in, joint torques out.
One big neural net.
OpenVLA, RT-2, PaLM-E—all doing this.
The embodied question you're really asking: Is there a fundamentally different neural architecture for physical reasoning vs text reasoning?
Yes and no. The transformer architecture works for both.
But embodied models have different training—they see video, proprioception (joint states), force feedback.
The representations they learn are grounded in physics, not just token statistics.
Everything Stack angle: Your trainable components could wrap either approach.
Classical IK solver as one component, neural behavior policy as another.
The semantic search finds relevant skills regardless of implementation.
You're not betting on one architecture—you're building the orchestration layer that coordinates whatever works.

Why 12-18 months for DIY advantage:

Because that's when mass production catches up.
Right now Unitree is doing thousands of units, not millions.
When they hit iPhone-scale manufacturing, the cost curve inverts—you can't compete with injection-molded parts and bulk motor procurement.
But *today* they're still iterating hardware, and your custom build is roughly equivalent capability at similar cost with more flexibility.

What you CAN'T do right now:
Match their motor power density (custom windings, proprietary gearboxes)
Match their battery integration (thermal management, BMS tuning)
Get the same sensor fusion they've spent years calibrating
Achieve their walking stability without months of RL training

What you CAN do:
Build a functional arm or upper body for manipulation tasks
Train behavior policies on your specific use cases
Iterate faster than their release cycle
Own the full stack

Electric (best modern): ~200-400 W/kg

System-level, the gap narrows.

Policy architecture:

It's the neural network structure that maps observation → action.
Baseline embodied intelligence: Sort of.
OpenVLA and RT-X are trained on ~1M robot trajectories across 22+ embodiments.
They've seen enough manipulation that they have priors about physics, object permanence, force application.
You fine-tune from there, not from scratch.
Think of it like: LLM pretraining gives you language priors, then you fine-tune for your task.
VLA pretraining gives you physics/manipulation priors, then you fine-tune for your specific robot and task.

Neural net directly to motor—the matrix question you're asking:

Yes.
Camera pixels (matrix) → neural net (matrix multiplications through transformer layers) → joint torques (vector).
No explicit IK, no PID in the middle.
The network learns the physics implicitly.
The "matrix of real world space" you're intuiting—that's the latent representation.
The network builds an internal model of 3D space, object positions, forces, all as high-dimensional vectors that get transformed through layers.
It's not *explicitly* a coordinate frame, but it *functions* like one.

VLA unpredictability/safety:

Yes, it's generative.
Yes, it could hurt things.

Why it's actually safer than you'd think:
Action space is bounded.
Joint torques have physical limits.
The network can't output "infinite force.

"
You clip outputs.
Any command outside safe envelope gets clamped.
Modern actuators are backdrivable—if the arm hits something unexpected, it gives rather than powers through.

Why it's still concerning:
Distribution shift.
Robot sees something it's never seen in training, outputs nonsense.
- Temporal compounding.
Small errors accumulate over action sequences.
- Adversarial inputs.
Weird lighting or reflections could trigger bad behavior.

Stopping it:

Easier in action space than intent space.
You can put hard limits on joint velocities, torques, workspace boundaries.
The robot *literally cannot* move faster than X or exert more than Y Newtons regardless of what the neural net wants.
That's not true for text generation—you can't hard-limit an LLM's semantic output.

Sensor fusion / bus architecture:

CAN bus is standard for joint-level communication.
1Mbps, robust, every automotive and industrial system uses it.
EtherCAT for higher bandwidth (100Mbps) when you need fast sensor data.
Unitree uses custom protocol over EtherCAT for their IMUs and force sensors.
The architecture: central compute (Jetson/x86) runs the neural net and high-level control.

Same concept as text embeddings, different modality.

VLA - Vision Language Action models.
These are neural networks that take in camera images plus a language instruction and output motor commands directly.
The current state: they work in constrained settings, maybe 70-80% success rate on trained tasks, drop to 30-40% on novel variations.
OpenVLA is the open source one, 7 billion parameters, trained on about a million robot trajectories from 22 different robot types.

You show it enough examples of "pick up the red block" with visual variations, it learns to generalize to new red blocks in new positions.
It fails when the situation differs too much from training data.
How VLA actually works internally: Image goes through a vision encoder, becomes a high-dimensional vector.
Language instruction goes through a text encoder, becomes another vector.
These get concatenated or cross-attended.
Then transformer layers process the combined representation.
The output head predicts action tokens, which decode to joint positions or velocities.

System identification versus learned adaptation.
System identification is the classical approach: move the robot through known motions, measure where it actually goes, fit a parametric model of the errors.
Learned adaptation skips the explicit model, the neural network just sees enough examples that it implicitly compensates.
System identification is more interpretable, learned adaptation handles weirder nonlinearities.

Air gives you compliance for free.

Electric motors with modern control and series elastic actuators can approximate pneumatic compliance while staying clean and quiet.

Motor fundamentals:

Newtons measure force, not force over time.
Torque (Newton-meters) is force times lever arm distance.
A motor rated at 25 Nm can apply 25 Newtons at 1 meter from the axis, or 250 Newtons at 0.1 meters.
Holding strength and moving strength are different.
Holding (static torque) is usually higher than moving (dynamic torque) because you don't fight inertia and friction losses.
Industrial servo motors for robot arms run 20-120 Nm depending on joint position.
Shoulder joints need more torque than wrist joints because they're lifting the weight of the entire arm plus payload.
A motor that can hold 10kg at full extension might only lift 5kg dynamically because of acceleration requirements.

Motor control signals:

Not on/off.
PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) for basic servos, which is digital but encodes analog-like values through duty cycle.
Industrial servos use current control, you command a target current which translates to torque.
The motor driver handles the fast switching, the controller just sends position or torque targets over CAN bus or EtherCAT at 100-1000 Hz.
So your neural net outputs "go to position X" or "apply torque Y", the low-level driver handles the electrical details.

The hierarchical neural net architecture you're describing:

Yes, this is exactly what some research is doing.
It's called hierarchical imitation learning or options framework.

You have:
High-level policy (the narrator/thinker): Takes language + scene, outputs subgoals in semantic space
Mid-level policy (motor group coordinator): Takes subgoal + proprioception, outputs trajectories per limb
Low-level policy (motor controller): Takes trajectory chunk, outputs joint commands

Each level runs at different frequencies.
High-level at 1-5 Hz (thinking speed), mid-level at 10-30 Hz (coordination speed), low-level at 100+ Hz (control speed).
Can you chain neural nets this way?
The output of one becomes the input to the next.
The trick is the interface, what representation flows between levels.
Options: raw numbers (joint angles), learned embeddings (latent vectors), or explicit semantic descriptions.
Most research uses learned embeddings because they compress information efficiently.

The octopus design:

Biologically accurate.
Octopus has distributed neural processing, each arm has significant local computation.
For robots, this maps to having small neural nets or classical controllers at each joint that handle local reflexes, while the central brain handles coordination.
The advantage: faster reaction to local disturbances without waiting for central processing.
The disadvantage: harder to train end-to-end, need to define the interfaces between levels.

Microcontroller necessity:

Still needed, but minimal.
The Jetson runs the neural net at 30-100 Hz, outputs target positions.
The microcontroller (ESP32, STM32) runs the PID loop at 1-10 kHz, handles encoder reading, current limiting, safety stops.
You could theoretically run everything on the Jetson but the real-time guarantees are better with dedicated motor control hardware.

10M parameter model: ~1ms inference

So practical limit is around 100-200M parameters for real-time control.

The fundamental unit you need to understand is torque, measured in Newton-meters.
Think of it this way: if you have a wrench that's one meter long and you push on the end with ten Newtons of force, you're applying ten Newton-meters of torque to whatever you're turning.
A motor rated at thirty Newton-meters can hold that same force at that same distance.
Now here's where it gets practical: your arm is about 0.4 meters from shoulder to hand.
To hold a seven kilogram weight at full extension, gravity pulls down with about seventy Newtons.
Multiply by 0.4 meters and you need twenty-eight Newton-meters just to hold it still.
To actually lift it, to accelerate it upward, you need more.
How much more depends on how fast you want to move.
If you want to move that seven kilos through a half meter arc in one second, you're accelerating at roughly two meters per second squared, which adds another fourteen Newtons of force requirement.
So now you need maybe thirty-five Newton-meters total.
This is why robot arms doing dynamic lifting need motors rated at one and a half to two times the static holding requirement.
The difference between hobby servos and industrial servos comes down to a few key things.
Hobby servos like the Dynamixel XM series use plastic or metal gears, have maybe thirty Newton-meters peak torque, cost a few hundred dollars, and wear out after a few thousand hours of heavy use.

Industrial servos from Kollmorgen or Maxon use frameless designs where the motor integrates directly into the joint, have harmonic drives or cycloidal reducers that handle a hundred plus Newton-meters with near-zero backlash, cost thousands of dollars per joint, run for tens of thousands of hours.
The real difference is in the reducer.
A harmonic drive has a flexible spline that engages with a wave generator, giving you gear ratios of fifty to one or higher with backlash under one arc-minute.
That precision is what lets industrial robots hit repeatability of plus or minus fifty microns instead of plus or minus one millimeter.
Current control versus PWM is about precision and smoothness.
PWM tells the motor to be on for some percentage of each cycle, which works fine for position holding but creates torque ripple during motion.
Current control directly regulates the electromagnetic field, giving you smooth torque output that's proportional to your command signal.
This matters for force-sensitive tasks.
If you're trying to apply exactly five Newtons of force while the arm contacts a surface, PWM will give you choppy oscillating force while current control gives you steady pressure.
Industrial robots doing polishing, grinding, or assembly absolutely need current control.

VLM as narrator: The VLM (Vision-Language Model) handles both vision AND language, so it's doing scene understanding plus intent parsing in one model.
Figure's Helix uses a 7B VLM that looks at cameras and understands "pick up the red cup" simultaneously.
The trajectory planner below it is a smaller specialized model that just does vision-to-action, no language reasoning.
So yes, two separate concerns: semantic understanding (VLM) and motor planning (visuomotor policy).
80M parameter at 200 Hz: The 80M model outputs joint position targets, not raw motor commands.
The motors receive those targets and their internal controllers (or your hybrid neural-PID) execute them.
200 Hz means the policy updates its target 200 times per second, giving very smooth motion.
The motors themselves can respond much faster (1-10 kHz internal loops).
Helix cost: Figure AI hasn't published pricing, it's not available for purchase.
They're deploying it in BMW factories under commercial contracts.

Subgoal and action durations - let me be precise here because you asked me to check you:

Looking at the actual research:
π0.5 predicts subtasks that span 2-10 seconds typically
The VLA outputs action chunks of 50-100 timesteps at 10-50 Hz, roughly 1-2 seconds of motion per inference
Motor group policies in Helix output at 200 Hz continuously, not in chunks

So the timing is: Narrator fires on task change or completion (variable, could be 5 seconds to 5 minutes).
VLA/trajectory runs every 0.5-2 seconds, outputting the next 1-2 seconds of motion.
Motor execution is continuous at 100-200 Hz.
Why not all running at the same timeframe: Different computational costs.
The narrator (8B params) takes 100-500ms to run.
The VLA (100-500M params) takes 30-100ms.
The motor group (5-50M) takes 5-10ms.
The joint controller (100K-1M + PID) takes 0.1-1ms.
If you tried to run the narrator at 200 Hz, you'd need impossible compute.
The hierarchy exists because different decisions need different amounts of thinking time.
Proprioception: Yes, it's the robot's sense of its own body position.
Joint angles, velocities, motor currents.
Not touch exactly, that's tactile sensing, but internal body awareness.
What makes robots slower on the production line: Not the control frequency.

It's:
Vision processing latency (30-100ms to understand a scene)
Conservatism in the policy (trained to be safe, not fast)
Settling time (waiting for vibrations to damp before precision moves)
Human-imposed speed limits for safety certification

Industrial robots CAN move extremely fast.
UR5 max speed is 1 m/s, some industrial arms hit 5+ m/s.
The limitation is usually the task, not the hardware.
Hidden units: Neurons in a layer that isn't input or output.
A 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units means: input layer → 32 neurons → 32 neurons → output layer.
Each hidden unit computes a weighted sum of inputs, applies a nonlinearity, passes to the next layer.
Zero-shot transfer: The MeMo paper trained a controller on a 6-legged robot.
Then they added 2 more legs to the simulation (8 legs total).
Without any additional training, the same per-joint policies worked because each joint's controller only sees local information.
The network didn't need to "learn" 8 legs because each leg's controller is independent.
That's what modular architecture enables.
Morphology: Body shape/structure.
A spider has different morphology than a humanoid.
Morphology transfer means a controller trained on one body shape working on a different body shape.
Is the narrator what creates subgoals: Yes, or an intermediate planner layer.
The narrator outputs structured intent like "pick up red block, place in bin" which might decompose into subgoals: (1) move to block, (2) grasp, (3) lift, (4) move to bin, (5) release.
Some systems do this decomposition explicitly (SayCan, π0.5), others let the VLA figure it out implicitly.

Bluetooth (BLE): Lower power, simpler pairing, but limited bandwidth (~2 Mbps practical).

WiFi: Higher bandwidth (50+ Mbps), lower latency (5-10ms vs 20-50ms BLE), but more power hungry and slightly more complex setup.
For your use case, WiFi is better.
